title: Load-to-Unload Principle
note: The lower half's job is to create a load in the pelvis so there is something to unload into rotation — without a load, the torso does all the work.

title: Rotational Hinge (3D winding)
note: True backside loading isn't just a sagittal hip-hinge — it's winding hip flexion + rotation together, loading the outer glute and deep hip rotators.

title: Hip IR Mover Type
note: Seated hip rotation test: <15° IR = tight mover, 15–30° = moderate, >30° = mobile. Determines realistic back-hip positions.

title: Loading From Above vs Below
note: Above = pelvis rotates over a relatively vertical shin (e.g. Chapman). Below = load comes from the femur/positive shin angle, pelvis stays neutral (e.g. Keller, Miller).

title: Tight Movers Still Need a Load
note: Guys with limited hip range won't get deep coil, but still need an attempt to load — coaching them to just "clear the front side" without loading can cost velocity.

title: Front Side Tension
note: Glove-side internal rotation/pronation tension pairs with backside tension — staying closed on both sides, not just the back hip.

title: Timing of the Load
note: Load timing varies by pitcher: preset at set position, at peak leg lift, or gathered during the stride.

title: Cross-Body Reach Feel
note: Wide stance, reach glove arm across the body as far as possible to feel where back-hip tension blocks out.

title: Stool / Swivel Chair Hinge Drill
note: Straddle a rolling stool, ride forward without letting the knee extend — teaches the feeling of winding tension as you move forward.

title: Hip IR Screen (Box + Foam Roller)
note: Seated, knees at 90°, foam roller between knees, rotate feet out to measure internal rotation range and bucket mover type.

title: 3D Strap Resisted Load
note: Band anchored and looped around hips, pulling into early rotation; pitcher resists while moving forward to build backside tension.

title: Sliding Hinge Drill
note: Slider under front foot lets the pitcher ride center mass forward in slow motion to feel the load build during the stride.

title: Band-Resisted Rotation (3-band setup)
note: Bands looped around hips bias early opening; pitcher resists to reinforce staying closed until the last second.

title: Front + Back Band Combo Drill
note: Band on hips plus a band pulling the throwing arm into early supination — resist both to train combined front/back tension.

title: Turn Back Foot In 15–25°
note: Simplest in-bullpen tweak — turning the back foot in biases extra internal rotation load at set position.

title: Hook the Rubber
note: Angling the back foot on the rubber to bias a more positive shin angle and backside load.

title: Counter-Rotation / Coil Drills (Janitor, Quick Pick, Rotational Stepback)
note: Start more closed/counter-rotated than normal to exaggerate the need to rotate through to the front leg.

title: Tension Rocker Drill
note: Reach to end-range tension, then perform a rocker throw starting from that loaded position.

title: Roll-In
note: Turning the back foot in during the delivery itself to exaggerate internal rotation load in the back leg.

title: "Winding the Spring"
note: Overall metaphor for building 3D backside tension that gets released into rotation.

title: Shot Put Comparison Test
note: Throw a 6lb med ball with zero hip load vs. a fired/loaded hip to feel the power difference tension creates.

title: Lead Leg Block Purpose
note: The lead leg is a stable anchor the pelvis rotates into, converting stride momentum into rotational energy up the chain.

title: Three Energy Leaks at Landing
note: Anterior-posterior (knee keeps sinking forward), vertical (sinks straight down), medial-lateral (knee/ankle bows out) — all bleed energy into the ground.

title: Pawback Mechanism
note: Borrowed from sprinting — the lead knee extends backward through ball release rather than just blocking statically.

title: Pelvis Drives Knee Extension
note: Lead leg extension should be a byproduct of hip rotation pulling the femur, not the quad actively firing or vaulting over the leg.

title: Lead Leg Should Be Automatic
note: Don't coach the front leg directly — fix rotation and back-hip loading, and the block tends to clean up on its own.

title: Hamstring ISO Hold (split stance)
note: Split stance stretch with active quad-contraction extensions and 10-second iso holds to open hip flexion for the front side.

title: Hip 90/90 IR Activation
note: 90/90 position with iso holds driving the foot down, then lifting up, to open and own new internal rotation range in the lead hip.

title: Hip Airplanes
note: Wall-assisted rotation-and-control drill training the outer glute to eccentrically decelerate the pelvis; progress with band or cable.

title: Rotational Kettlebell Swing (diagonal)
note: Diagonal-pattern KB swing from a split stance that overloads the outer glute's deceleration role.

title: Medicine Ball Wall Taps
note: Split-stance (then single-leg) rotational wall taps to build front-foot stability and proprioception.

title: 3D Strap 360° Turn
note: Weighted 360° turn into a band pulling forward — teaches the front leg to stabilize against rotational pull instead of collapsing.

title: Ipsilateral Cable Row
note: Same-side row driven by back-hip rotation rather than the arm — reinforces hip-driven pulling pattern, can be heavily loaded.

title: Daddy Hack / Swing Feel Drill
note: Use an imaginary bat swing to access a ground-based rotation pattern most guys already own, then bridge it into throwing.

title: Diagonal Medicine Ball Chop (off a box/slope)
note: Diagonal chop from an elevated stance to mimic the downhill oblique sling into the lead leg, low effort from the arms.

title: Lasso Drill (no stride, no arm swing)
note: Strips out leg lift, stride, and arm action — isolates loading the back hip and unloading into the front leg.

title: Lasso Drill Constraints (hurdle / band / elevated front foot)
note: Add a hurdle in front of the knee, resistance band pulling open, or an elevated front foot to correct specific leaks in the lasso drill.

title: Rocker Throw / Figure-8 Rocker
note: Adds full arm action back into the isolated back-hip loading pattern; figure-8 path helps some pitchers stop overthinking the arm.

title: Janitor Throw / Drop Step / Turn-and-Burn
note: Start facing away or heavily closed off, then rotate through — exaggerates the rotational requirement for pitchers who struggle to rotate.

title: "Throw the Belly Button Into the Lead Leg"
note: Simple rotational cue used during the lasso drill to keep focus on the hips, not the arm.

title: "Feed the Flaw"
note: Using resistance bands to exaggerate the exact fault (early opening) so the body learns to resist and hold tension longer.

title: Instant Clicks vs. Long-Term Gains
note: Most velocity development happens over months/years, but occasional mechanical "clicks" can produce real 1–3 mph jumps in a single session — hacks are things to test, not guarantees.

title: Blind Split-Testing Protocol
note: Throw ~10 reps per variation at consistent sub-max effort without knowing the radar numbers; have a partner track results to find real (not placebo) differences.

title: Back Foot Angle Test
note: Split test in/neutral/out/hooked back foot angle on the rubber. Outward tends to suit external-rotation-dominant, vertical-shin guys; inward suits internal-rotation-dominant guys.

title: Rubber Position / Stride Direction Test
note: Split test starting arm-side, middle, or glove-side on the rubber to influence stride direction, timing, and arm sync.

title: Fastball Grip Split-Test
note: Test four-seam vs. two-seam, finger width, and thumb position (side / tucked / under) for velocity and movement-profile differences.

title: Intent & PAP (Post-Activation Potentiation)
note: Deliberately increasing effort helps some pitchers and causes others to "muscle up" and lose sequencing. For guys who can't turn it on in practice, a short max-effort primer (isometrics, med ball throws, jumps) can prime the CNS before throwing.

title: Tempo (Peak Leg Lift to Release)
note: Standardized measure of delivery speed from peak leg lift to ball release. Too slow (roughly 25+ frames) lets energy bleed and inefficiency creep in; too fast doesn't let the lower half load — cueing tempo up or down depending on the athlete can produce a quick velo bump.

title: Old-School Wind-Up / Hands-Over-the-Head Cue
note: Even for stretch-only pitchers, training wind-up work with a hands-over-the-head cue can fix upper/lower half sequencing and restore athletic smoothness.

title: Workload / Fatigue Masking Fitness
note: Chronic under-recovery — especially recovery-day throwing, pregame bullpen/long toss volume, and in-season lifting volume — quietly suppresses velocity. Auditing and trimming it can produce a quick spike.

title: The Drift
note: The initial center-of-mass shift away from the back leg during leg lift, creating room for an active drive phase. Without it, a pitcher just falls toward the target instead of driving.

title: Coil-and-Drift vs. Straight-On-Target Drift
note: Two drift styles: a coiled/counter-rotated timing mechanism (e.g. a Chapman-type mover) versus a straighter, dynamic move to a forward balance point (e.g. a deGrom-type mover).

title: Balance Point Isn't Required
note: Some elite, hard throwers stay back and never drift — it's common among the hardest throwers, but not universal, and shouldn't be forced on everyone.

title: Drift Is the Icing, Not the Foundation
note: Only layer in the drift once major sequencing issues (hip/shoulder separation, arm timing, front leg bracing) are already solid — it can hurt pitchers who already rely on a stable balance point.

title: "Lean Into the Leg Lift"
note: Simplest cue to initiate the drift — shift weight slightly forward during leg lift without losing touch with the back leg.

title: Hit Balance Point 4–6 Inches Out
note: Aim the peak leg lift position several inches further from the rubber than normal, keeping everything else about the delivery the same.

title: Rotate 15° Toward the Target
note: Alternative framing of the same forward weight-shift cue — rotate the body slightly toward the target during leg lift instead of staying square.

title: "Stay Inside the Back Foot"
note: Keep weight from settling fully onto the heel during leg lift, allowing an early, subtle forward shift.

title: Step-Back Wind-Up Drill
note: Come set, take a step back, then execute the leg lift and throw. Teaches staying inside the back foot and building forward momentum without the excessive lean-back that walking wind-ups can cause.
